content:
Hi,

I was very pleasantly surprised that it has become possible to prove properties about while loops.

I had expected that a verifiable implementation of while would take much longer to arrive. I think this is excellent work, and I would like to express my appreciation to the developers.

That said, I have one request about while statements.

When execution exits a while loop normally, that is, not by break, the loop condition should be false. However, it seems that currently this proof is not available inside the body of the surrounding function.

def exampleFun (n : Nat) : Nat := Id.run do
  let mut m := n
  while h : m > 0 do
    m := m - 1
  have : m = 0 := by
    sorry
  return m

In this example, after the while loop terminates normally, we should know that ¬ m > 0, and hence be able to prove m = 0.

So I would like to have some way to access a proof that the loop condition is false when a while loop exits normally, excluding cases such as early exits by break.
@Sebastian Graf I think you are a developer of new do elaborator

So you expect to have an additional assumption h : ¬ m > 0 in your context depending on whether the while body contains a break? I'd say this is quite orthogonal to the "verifiable while loops" feature, and I find it somewhat strange in the sense that presence of break or continue shouldn't really influence the local context...

This is an extension of the

def foo : IO Unit := do
  if h : P then
    foo h
    return
  bar
  -- do we have `h : ¬P` here since `return` is in the `then`?

request I guess

Yes, that may indeed be the case. It is strange for the local context to change depending on the presence of break.

So does this mean that, in order to achieve what I want, I have no choice but to use some workaround, such as rewriting the loop using if expressions and recursion?
You can populate an Option (PLift P) in the loop, maybe

@Sebastian Graf

By the way, this is unrelated to the current topic, but I have one more question.

When using a while loop, it seems that partial is not required regardless of whether termination can be proved. I find this a little confusing, because this gives it a different UI from ordinary function definitions. Normally, when defining a recursive function, Lean reports an error if termination is not obvious.

When I heard that while loops had become verifiable, I expected that a while loop whose termination is not obvious would produce an error unless it was marked partial, but in fact that is not the case. Why is the specification different between while loops and general recursion? Is this difference essential?

Personally, I would prefer it if partial were required when termination cannot be proved, since that would feel more consistent.

So does this mean that, in order to achieve what I want, I have no choice but to use some workaround, such as rewriting the loop using if expressions and recursion?

Yes, that's right.

When using a while loop, it seems that partial is not required regardless of whether termination can be proved. I find this a little confusing, because this gives it a different UI from ordinary function definitions.

I can see that this might be confusing. But partial is not transitive; indeed, the old and the new while are both backed by a partial def under the hood; users never needed to annotate their using definition as partial before either, so it's not a new thing.

Furthermore, the farer we manage to push the partial "inside", the better; we might be able to prove properties about a function for which we do not need to reason about the partial intermediate result.

When I heard that while loops had become verifiable, I expected that a while loop whose termination is not obvious would produce an error unless it was marked partial, but in fact that is not the case. Why is the specification different between while loops and general recursion? Is this difference essential?

We'll have syntax like while ... decreasing_by ... do ... soon. That would built in the termination proof. I guess you are suggesting that users are forced to write something like partial while ... do ... when they don't provide a decreasing_by clause? Sounds plausible on the green field, but it feels like too much of an unforced breaking change...
Perhaps partial while could be made legal, and a linter option could be used to determine whether bare while without an (inferred) decreasing_by is a warning?

I see. Indeed, given that partial is not transitive, it is preferable to push partial further inside. I agree with what you are saying.

I’m looking forward to the implementation of while … decreasing_by and while … termination_by.

If termination is proved that way, does that mean that when proving something with mvcgen, I will no longer have to prove termination separately?

a linter option

Good idea! Or maybe a warning that's off by default...

If termination is proved that way, does that mean that when proving something with mvcgen, I will no longer have to prove termination separately?

Yes! If you provide the measure inline and prove the body decreasing in it, the goal is that you'll no longer need to redo it in vcgen proofs.
Sounds great! It’s wonderful to see mvcgen becoming even more feature-rich.
